{{Transformation rules}}

'''Negation introduction''' is a [[rule of inference]], or [[transformation rule]], in the field of [[propositional calculus]].

Negation introduction states that if a given antecedent implies both the consequent and its complement, then this implies the negated antecedent.<ref>{{cite book|editor-last=Wansing |editor-first=Heinrich|title=Negation: A Notion in Focus|date=1996|publisher=Walter de Gruyter|location=Berlin|isbn=3110147696}}</ref><ref>
{{cite book|last=Haegeman|first=Lilliane|title=The Syntax of Negation|url=https://archive.org/details/syntaxofnegation0000haeg|url-access=registration|date=30 Mar 1995|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge|isbn=0521464927|page=[https://archive.org/details/syntaxofnegation0000haeg/page/70 70]}}</ref> 

==Formal notation==
This can be written as:
:<math>\Big((P \rightarrow Q) \land (P \rightarrow \neg Q)\Big) \rightarrow \neg P </math>

An example of its use would be an attempt to prove two contradictory statements from a single fact. For example, if a person were to state "Whenever I hear the phone ringing I am happy" and then state "Whenever I hear the phone ringing I am ''not'' happy", one can infer that the person never hears the phone ringing.

Many [[proofs by contradiction]] use negation introduction as reasoning scheme: to prove ¬''P'', assume for contradiction ''P'', then derive from it two contradictory inferences ''Q'' and ¬''Q''. Since the latter contradiction renders ''P'' impossible, ¬''P'' must hold.

==Proof==
With <math>\neg P</math> identified as <math>P\to\bot</math>, the principle is as a special case of [[Frege's theorem]], already in [[minimal logic]].

Another derivation makes use of <math>A\to \neg B</math> as the [[currying|curried]], equivalent form of <math>\neg (A \land B)</math>. Using this twice, the principle is seen equivalent to the negation of 
<math>\big(P\land(P\to Q)\big)\land \neg(P\and Q)</math>
which, via modus ponens and rules for conjunctions, is itself equivalent to the valid noncontradiction principle for <math>P\and Q</math>.

A classical derivation passing through the introduction of a disjunction may be given as follows:
{| class="wikitable"
! ''Step''
! ''Proposition''
! ''Derivation''
|-
| 1 || <math>(P \to Q)\land(P \to \neg Q)</math> || Given
|-
| 2 || <math>(\neg P \lor Q)\land(\neg P \lor \neg Q)</math> || Classical equivalence of the [[Material implication (rule of inference)|material implication]]
|-
| 3 || <math>\neg P \lor (Q \land \neg Q)</math> || Distributivity
|-
| 4 || <math>\neg P \lor \bot</math> || [[Law of noncontradiction]] for <math>Q</math>
|-
| 5 || <math>\neg P</math> || [[Disjunctive syllogism]] (3,4)
|}
